abstract: This lecture presents five cases of pelvic pain, emphasizing a systematic approach using seven historical features: onset, location, quality, cyclicity, duration, radiation, and aggravating/relieving factors. The speaker highlights how patterns in these features can diagnose conditions like endometriosis and adenomyosis without labs or imaging, relying on clinical reasoning. Key points include differentiating primary from secondary dysmenorrhea, recognizing that endometriosis often improves with pregnancy due to progesterone dominance, and diagnosing adenomyosis by cyclic midline pain with a boggy, tender premenstrual uterus. Physical exam findings like decreased uterine mobility suggest adhesive disease from endometriosis.
key_points: Use seven historical features (onset, location, quality, cyclicity, duration, radiation, aggravators/relievers) to define patterns in pelvic pain.
Cyclic pain associated with menstruation or ovulation points to a gynecologic cause like endometriosis or adenomyosis.
Pregnancy suppresses endometriosis via progesterone dominance, reducing endometrial proliferation and pain.
Birth control pills (progesterone-dominant) are first-line treatment for progestin-responsive endometriosis.
Secondary dysmenorrhea changes over time (worsens) and affects daily activities, unlike primary dysmenorrhea.
Decreased uterine mobility on pelvic exam suggests adhesive disease, commonly from endometriosis or prior PID.
Adenomyosis presents with cyclic midline pain, heavy menses, and a boggy, tender uterus premenstrually; history alone suffices for diagnosis.
Deep dyspareunia that is constant and non-cyclic suggests anatomic issues like scarring from endometriosis.
Bowel or bladder symptoms (e.g., pain with defecation, urinary frequency) may indicate uterine pathology impacting adjacent organs.
Endometriosis can be diagnosed 85% of the time by history alone without labs or imaging, relying on pattern recognition.
